description: 100 deep logical questions on abstraction in Python OOP

questions.answer:
Output: `Can't instantiate abstract class Shape without an implementation for abstract method 'area'`

ABC uses the ABCMeta metaclass; when its `__new__` finishes building a class whose `__abstractmethods__` is non-empty, the instantiation call path raises `TypeError` before an object ever exists. Every method decorated with `@abstractmethod` gets the flag `__isabstractmethod__ = True`, and the metaclass collects all such names inherited through the MRO into the class attribute `__abstractmethods__`; if that frozenset is non-empty, calling the class raises exactly this TypeError.

Output: `Can't instantiate abstract class Broken without an implementation for abstract method 'run'`

The metaclass computes a subclass's abstract methods as the union of the abstract sets of all bases, then subtracts any name that the subclass overrides in its own `__dict__`. `Broken` overrides nothing, so `Broken.__abstractmethods__ == frozenset({'run'})`, and instantiating raises TypeError even though `Broken` is a subclass of `Base`. Note only the *missing* method is reported; implemented names are dropped from the set and never listed.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
```python
from abc import ABC

class Marker(ABC):
    pass

m = Marker()
print(type(m).__name__)
```
questions.answer:
Output: `Marker`

An ABC with no abstract methods is perfectly instantiable. `ABC` only installs the `ABCMeta` metaclass; the metaclass's enforcement triggers solely when `__abstractmethods__` is non-empty. `Marker.__abstractmethods__` is `frozenset()`, so the class behaves like a normal class. This is why "abstract class" really means "class with a non-empty `__abstractmethods__`", not "inherits from ABC".

Output: `True 4 frozenset()`

When `Square` defines `area`, the metaclass sees that name in `Square.__dict__` and removes it from the inherited abstract set, leaving `frozenset()`. The class is now concrete and instantiable. `isinstance(s, Shape)` is `True` because `Square` is a real subclass in the MRO — implementing the abstract methods is what makes it a legal concrete subclass. ABCs are designed to be used with `isinstance`/`issubclass` for formal interface checking.

Output: `Can't instantiate abstract class B without an implementation for abstract method 'run' | frozenset({'run'})`

Abstractness propagates automatically down the hierarchy: `B` inherits the abstract `run` from `A`, and the metaclass's union rule keeps it in `B.__abstractmethods__`. Since `B` defines nothing in its own namespace that shadows `run`, the abstract status is preserved across any number of intermediate classes. A subclass stays abstract until every name in the inherited abstract set is overridden somewhere in its MRO.

Output: `go frozenset({'run'}) frozenset()`

`B` still does not override `run`, so it remains abstract with `__abstractmethods__ == frozenset({'run'})`. The grandchild `C` finally supplies an override; the metaclass finds `run` in `C.__dict__` and subtracts it from the union of `A`'s and `B`'s abstract sets, making `C` concrete. `B` and `C` each get their own freshly computed `__abstractmethods__`; concrete status is decided per-class, not per-branch.

Output: `left`

`Bottom` instantiates successfully even though `Right` never implemented `f`. The metaclass clears the abstract set with `getattr(cls, name, None)` — attribute lookup walks the MRO `Bottom -> Left -> Right -> Root`, finds `Left.f`, sees it is concrete (`__isabstractmethod__` falsy), and removes the name from the union. Because `Left` precedes `Right` in the MRO, its implementation satisfies the interface for the whole class. This shows abstract handling is name-based through normal attribute resolution, not per-branch accounting.

Output: `Can't instantiate abstract class Comb without an implementation for abstract method 'f'`

The two abstract declarations have the same name `f`, and `__abstractmethods__` is a set, so the union collapses them into one entry. A single implementation in the subclass satisfies both bases: `class Subst(Comb): def f(self): return 1` would instantiate fine. This is how you implement an interface that multiple ABCs agree on — one method fulfills all of them.

Blank 1 (outermost/top) = `staticmethod`, blank 2 (innermost/bottom) = `abstractmethod`, i.e. `@staticmethod` above `@abstractmethod`.

`@abstractmethod` sets a writable `__isabstractmethod__` flag on the function; `@staticmethod` then wraps the flagged function in a `staticmethod` object. The metaclass calls `getattr(type(...), '__isabstractmethod__', False)` on the *result* of the composed decorators, and `staticmethod` objects propagate the flag. In the reverse order `@abstractmethod` tries to write `__isabstractmethod__` onto an already-existing `staticmethod` object, whose attribute is read-only — raising `AttributeError: attribute '__isabstractmethod__' of 'staticmethod' objects is not writable`.

Output: `AttributeError: attribute '__isabstractmethod__' of 'staticmethod' objects is not writable`

Decorator application is bottom-up: `@staticmethod` runs first, converting the plain function into a `staticmethod` descriptor object. The outer `@abstractmethod` then tries to set `__isabstractmethod__` on that descriptor via `setattr`, but a `staticmethod`'s attribute table is not mutable, so it raises `AttributeError`. The class is never created, proving the correct composition is `@staticmethod` on top and `@abstractmethod` underneath.

Output: `made made`

`@classmethod` is outermost and `@abstractmethod` innermost, the legal order. `create` is abstract in `Factory`; `Maker` overrides it with a concrete classmethod, so `Maker.__abstractmethods__` becomes empty and the class instantiates. Accessing it via the class (`Maker.create()`) and via an instance (`Maker().create()`) both resolve to the same bound classmethod and both print `made`.

Output: `abstract body`

Calling the classmethod `Stub.create()` does NOT raise TypeError — it simply calls the inherited abstract stub and returns `'abstract body'`. The abstractness guard fires only when the *class itself is instantiated* (`Stub()`), because that is where ABCMeta checks `__abstractmethods__`. A classmethod call never constructs an instance of the class object that stores `__abstractmethods__`, so the inherited abstract body is dispatched to directly. (If the stub body were just `...`, the call would return `None`.) This is a subtle trap: you can invoke abstract methods through the class object without ever triggering the abstract-interface error.

Output: `Can't instantiate abstract class Ghost without an implementation for abstract method 'name'`

`@property` above `@abstractmethod` produces an abstract property object (its `fget` carries `__isabstractmethod__ = True`). `Ghost` provides nothing in its own `__dict__`, so the name `name` stays in `__abstractmethods__`. Abstract properties behave exactly like abstract methods: any class forgetting to re-define the property is non-instantiable and is listed by name in the error.

Output: `maan frozenset()`

The metaclass only cares that the name `name` is overridden in the subclass namespace; it never checks that the override is itself a property. `name = 'maan'` shadows the abstract property, which removes the name from `__abstractmethods__`, so instantiation succeeds and `m.name` resolves to the class attribute value `maan`. Be aware this silently destroys the getter/setter behavior — future `x.name = v` just creates an instance attribute (or fails under `__slots__`).

Output: `<bound method Sly.name of <__main__.Sly object at 0x...>>` (the print emits a bound-method repr, not `'method'`)

There is no TypeError: the metaclass resolves the abstract sibling by name and sees `Sly.name` is overridden, so `__abstractmethods__` is empty and `Sly` instantiates. But because the override is a plain function and not a property, attribute access `s.name` calls it as a normal method, yielding a bound-method object (whose repr is printed). Accessing `s.name() is actually irrelevant here` — the unbundled call `s.name` is the bound method itself; to retrieve the string you would need `s.name()`. The abstract contract said "property", but Python only enforces the name, not the descriptor kind.

Output: `AttributeError: attribute '__isabstractmethod__' of 'property' objects is not writable`

Bottom-up decoration: `@property` first wraps the function into a `property` descriptor, then the outer `@abstractmethod` tries to `setattr` `__isabstractmethod__` on that property object. `property` instances use an immutable attribute layout, so the write fails immediately with `AttributeError` during class-body execution. Therefore for properties the only valid order is `@property` outermost and `@abstractmethod` innermost.

Output:
```
D!
Can't instantiate abstract class Empty without an implementation for abstract method '__str__'
```

Special/dunder methods can be abstract just like any other method. `Done` overrides `__str__` concretely, so `Done.__abstractmethods__` is empty and `str(Done())` returns `D!`. `Empty` inherits the abstract `__str__` untouched, keeping `'__str__'` in its abstract set, so constructing it raises the standard TypeError. The abstract body `return 'stub-str'` in the ABC is only a placeholder and never runs through normal dispatch.

Output:
```
impl ctor
base ctor
```

`Impl` overrides the abstract `__init__`, clearing it from `__abstractmethods__`, so `Impl()` instantiates. Inside the concrete constructor `super().__init__()` finds `Base.__init__` through the MRO and invokes it, executing the body. This works because `@abstractmethod` is only a flag; it does not destroy the underlying function. The bodies of abstract methods remain callable via `super()` from concrete implementations.

Output: `[BREAKING]`

The abstract `title` has no runnable body of its own (just `...`), yet `render()` calls `self.title()` and works perfectly because of dynamic dispatch: at runtime `self` is a `News` instance, so the call resolves to the concrete override, which returns `'BREAKING'`. This is the template method pattern — the ABC fixes the algorithm's skeleton (`render`) while subclasses plug in the variable steps (`title`). The abstract step could never run as-is anyway, since the ABC cannot be instantiated.

Output:
```
boot:
ready
```

`Boot.__init__` already executes *after* `Impl` was created, and by then `self` is a fully realized `Impl` whose `pre` is concrete, so the call dispatches to it and prints `ready`. There is no abstractness at call time; the TypeError guard only fires while a class with a non-empty `__abstractmethods__` is being instantiated. This makes template/pyramid initialization safe: subclass hooks are usable inside the base constructor.

Output: `base-stub!`

`@abstractmethod` is a pure flag (`__isabstractmethod__ = True`); the function body is untouched. `B` overrides `greet` (clearing the flag for `B`), and inside it `super().greet()` walks the MRO to `A.greet`, calling the stub body which returns `'base-stub'`. The result is concatenated with `'!'`. Only the *abstractness marker* is consumed by the override — the decorated function remains perfectly callable through superclass lookup.

Output:
```
instantiated OK
runtime NotImplementedError
TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class HardSub without an implementation for abstract method 'process'
```

`NotImplementedError`-in-a-method is a *runtime* contract: nothing checks it until the method is actually called, and the class instantiates freely (`SoftSub` succeeded). `@abstractmethod` is a *class-construction-time* contract enforced by the metaclass: `HardSub` is rejected the moment you try to instantiate it, before any method call. They also differ in intent — `NotImplementedError` is documentation-by-exception for optional/partial behavior, whereas abstract methods force subclasses to provide a real implementation.

questions.question:
What does `@abstractmethod` do when the class does NOT use `ABC`/`ABCMeta`? Predict the output:
```python
from abc import abstractmethod

class Loose:
    @abstractmethod
    def work(self):
        return 'loose work'

l = Loose()
print(l.work())
print(getattr(Loose, '__abstractmethods__', 'missing'))
```
questions.answer:
Output:
```
loose work
missing
```

`@abstractmethod` is just a marker that stores `__isabstractmethod__ = True` on the function; nothing enforces it unless the class is built by `ABCMeta`. `Loose` has the default `type` metaclass, so the flag is inert: the class instantiates, the method runs, and there is no `__abstractmethods__` attribute at all. This is why it is a bug to sprinkle `@abstractmethod` on a class that does not inherit from `ABC` — you silently get zero enforcement.

Output: `Can't instantiate abstract class Manual without an implementation for abstract method 'go'`

`ABC` is literally a convenience subclass whose only job is to add `metaclass=abc.ABCMeta`; using the metaclass directly is equivalent. `Manual` gets its `__abstractmethods__` computed by the same metaclass machinery, so instantiation raises the identical TypeError. Everything that applies to `class X(ABC)` applies here — dtype: abstract methods, abstract properties, and inheritance propagation all behave the same way.

Output: `p e`

`Hybrid` merges a normal concrete base `Plain` with the ABC mixin: concrete methods from `Plain` are inherited normally, and `Hybrid` itself remains abstract because of `extra`. `Impl` implements `extra`, clearing the abstract set, so it instantiates and has both methods available. The metaclass follows the full MRO when computing abstractness, so mixing styles costs nothing as long as every abstract name gets an override reachable through the MRO.

Output:
```
True
True
[]
```

`Shape.register(Defacto)` enters `Defacto` into ABCMeta's internal virtual-subclass registry (a set tied to the ABC's cache token), so both `isinstance` and `issubclass` return `True`. But `Defacto` is not a real child: it does not appear in `Shape.__subclasses__()`, it is not in `Shape`'s MRO, and it is not granted any attributes. Registration is also unchecked — `Shape.register` would accept a class with no `area` at all.

Output:
```
False
True
```

Even though `Circle` structurally has an `area` method, `isinstance` against an ABC is based on real inheritance or explicit registration — duck typing alone does not count. The first check is `False`. After `Shape.register(Circle)`, the class is a virtual subclass, so the same `isinstance` becomes `True`. This is the key contrast between *structural* duck typing and *formal* interfaces: ABCs let you opt specific classes in explicitly rather than guessing from method presence.

Output:
```
True False
True
Duckish
```

`__subclasshook__` replaces inheritance: when `ABCMeta.__subclasshook__` is called (as it is by every `issubclass`/`isinstance`), your method inspects the candidate's MRO and returns `True` for a structural match. `RealDuck` has `quack`, so it is treated as a subclass without ever inheriting; `Dog` lacks it and gets `False`. The `if cls is Duckish` guard plus `return NotImplemented` defers subclasses of the ABC to default checks. `Duckish` itself has no abstract methods, so `Duckish()` instantiates.

Output: `9`

`Impl` supplies a complete property object with fget and fset, so `'val'` is dropped from `Impl.__abstractmethods__` and instantiation succeeds. Assignment `r.val = 9` routes through the setter and the getter returns the stored value. The abstract contract only demanded a `val` attribute implemented in the subclass; whether that implementation is a property with one or both accessors (or anything else) is left to the implementer.

Output: `Can't instantiate abstract class M without an implementation for abstract methods 'alpha', 'zeta'`

The metaclass stores abstract names in a frozenset and the error routine joins them in *sorted* (alphabetical) order — `alpha` comes before `zeta` regardless of declaration order. Note the message switches from `abstract method '<name>'` (singular) to `abstract methods '<a>', '<b>'` (plural) when more than one name is missing. Parsing this message for test assertions is fragile; prefer checking `__abstractmethods__` directly.

Output: `Can't instantiate abstract class U without an implementation for abstract method 'y'`

`U` removes `x` from its abstract set by implementing it, then *adds* a new abstract method `y` with its own `@abstractmethod` decoration. The final `__abstractmethods__` is `frozenset({'y'})`, and only that one missing name is reported. This layering — resolve some obligations, impose new ones — is how abstract intermediate classes carve out design steps while leaving the remaining work to their children.

Output:
```
U.__abstractmethods__ = frozenset({'f'})
TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class U without an implementation for abstract method 'f'
```

The cheat fails: `ABCMeta.__new__` *recomputes and overwrites* `__abstractmethods__` after the class body runs, discarding the manually assigned empty frozenset. It evaluates `getattr(U, 'f')` through the MRO, sees the abstract stub, and builds `frozenset({'f'})`. `__abstractmethods__` is computed metadata, not idle state you can seed. The legit way to make a class concrete is to actually override the method.

questions.question:
But the *same* overwriting happens after class creation. Can you cheat at runtime by assigning afterwards? Predict the output:
```python
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def m(self):
        ...

class B(A):
    pass

B.__abstractmethods__ = frozenset()
b = B()
print('instantiated:', b)
print('m() returns:', b.m())
```
questions.answer:
Output:
```
instantiated: <__main__.B object at 0x...>
m() returns: None
```

Assigning `B.__abstractmethods__ = frozenset()` *after* the metaclass ran does take effect, because the instantiation-time guard reads the attribute from the class. So `B()` works and prints the object repr. The fraud shows its teeth on the call: `B.m` is still the original abstract stub (whose body is just `...`), so `b.m()` returns `None`. Abstractness is checked once at construction, not baked into the method's callability — hacks of this kind are fragile and should never ship.

Output: `f 7`

There is no conflict: the abstractness logic operates purely on class attributes and the metaclass, never on instance `__dict__` layout. The ABC declares the abstract `f`; `Impl` supplies it and adds its own slot `x`. Because `f` is a real method (a descriptor in class `__dict__`), not an instance attribute, `__slots__` restrictions do not interfere. Both the method call and slot assignment work exactly as in a plain class.

Output: `static static`

Yes. The metaclass only checks that the name `do` is overridden in the subclass namespace; it does not require the same descriptor kind. Replacing an instance method with a staticmethod clears `__abstractmethods__`, so `StatImpl()` works. Both access paths — through the instance `s.do()` and through the class `StatImpl.do()` — resolve to the same static function and print `static`. You can mix descriptor kinds between interface and implementation freely.

Output:
```
hi
frozenset()
```

Abstractness is purely name-based: overriding `echo` at all clears it, whatever its parameter signature. `Short.echo(msg)` accepts only one argument while the interface advertised two, and Python raises no error — a genuine `TypeError` would only appear at call time if someone passed `loud=`. This means ABCs document *what* must exist, not *how* it must be called; signature enforcement (e.g. via static analysis) is outside the language's reach here.

Output:
```
mid leaf
frozenset({'r'})
frozenset({'m'})
frozenset()
```

Each class's frozen set is computed independently from its own MRO: `Root` still shows `{'r'}` (it never implements anything), `Mid` implements `r` but adds abstract `m`, so it shows `{'m'}`, and `Leaf` implements everything, so it is empty. The per-class snapshots let you inspect a class's remaining obligations at any level — useful for plugin frameworks that want to report "what is still missing on this abstract layer".

Output:
```
True True True
frozenset() frozenset()
```

Because `B` implemented `a`, both `B` and `C` have empty `__abstractmethods__` and are concrete. `isinstance` on an ABC checks real subclass membership (or registration), so `C` is reported as an instance of every ancestor, including the abstract root `A`. 'Abstract' never affects identity checks after the implementation exists — the ABC stays a bona-fide supertype of all its concrete descendants.

Output:
```
True
False
```

`S2.area` is still the original stub function created by `@abstractmethod`, so its flag is `True`. `Impl.area` is a fresh, plain function the subclass wrote, so the flag is `False`. The metaclass uses exactly this attribute when computing new classes' abstract sets: it walks each class's names and checks `getattr(value, '__isabstractmethod__', False)`. You can likewise read the flag manually to test whether a method is still considered abstract.

Output:
```
False
True
False
```

`Fake` is a perfect duck — it has `run` — yet the ABC refuses to see it: formal checks ignore method presence and rely on inheritance or explicit registration. `Real`, which genuinely inherits and implements, passes both checks. That is the practical difference: duck typing accepts whatever quacks at call time, while ABCs give you an explicit, auditable contract you can test with `isinstance`/`issubclass`. Neither approach stops a wrong object at runtime unless you add the check yourself.

Output:
```
function
stub body ran
```

`Shape.area` is fetched from the class object — a plain function — and calling it is legal; the class never has to be instantiated for this. `abstractmethod` does not make the function uncallable, it only marks it. The stub body runs and returns 0 (which the call ignores). This is the mechanism behind `super().abstract_method()` working from concrete subclasses: the decorated body stays a normal, callable function.

Output: `True True False False`

Registration is bound to exactly the ABC it was called on: `X` becomes a virtual subclass of `A` only. When checking against `B`, ABCMeta consults `B`'s own virtual-subclass table and its `__subclasshook__`, walking `B`'s MRO but not treating `A`'s registry as `B`'s. So `isinstance(X(), B)` and `issubclass(X, B)` are both `False`. Unlike real inheritance, virtual subclassing does NOT propagate down the ABC family tree — each ABC keeps its own isolated registry.

Output: `real safe`

Both abstract stubs are legal; neither body matters — `WithBody` is non-instantiable due to the non-empty `__abstractmethods__`, and the enforcement point is class instantiation, not the bodies. Once `Impl` overrides both names, its abstract set is empty and both calls dispatch to the concrete implementations, printing `real safe`. Returning a value from an abstract stub (`'stub-result'`) and raising from another are both fine; the flag alone is what drives the metaclass's rejection.

Output:
```
csv loaded
<class 'abc.JsonLoader'>
Can't instantiate abstract class JsonLoader without an implementation for abstract method 'load'
```

The bug: `JsonLoader` declares no body and overrides nothing, so it silently inherits the abstract `load`. The intermediate `print(plugin := ...)` creates an equivalent dynamic subclass with the same problem (printing its repr is fine). The moment anyone tries `JsonLoader()`, the metaclass refuses with the standard TypeError naming `load`. Because nothing failed at *definition* time, an abstract class can ship unnoticed until it is used — always grep `__abstractmethods__` when a plugin class misbehaves at construction.

Output: `True`

This composition is already correct and there is no error here: `@staticmethod` outermost, `@abstractmethod` innermost is the only legal order. `abstractmethod` first flags the function in its `__isabstractmethod__`, then `staticmethod` wraps the flagged function into a descriptor that Python's tools treat as abstract (modern ABCMeta reads the attribute through the wrapper). The snippet in the prompt fails only when the orders are swapped. `Make` cannot be instantiated as-is; a subclass must override `build` (concretely, with its own staticmethod) to become concrete.

Output: `from I2`

`C` is concrete and instantiates. The metaclass resolves `f` from `C` via its MRO — `C -> I1 -> I2` — using `getattr`, finds `I2.f` which is concrete, and clears the name from the abstract set contributed by `I1`. This is the same MRO-collapsing behavior seen in diamonds: any implementation reachable through attribute lookup satisfies the contract for the whole class. `I1` itself remains abstract; abstractness is always decided per-class based on the full MRO.

Output:
```
AttributeError: 'Client' object has no attribute '__abstractmethods__'
```

Careful: classes built by a normal metaclass (like `type`) do not define `__abstractmethods__` at all, and `register()` does not add it. `Client.__abstractmethods__` raises `AttributeError`. Had the line been printed as `Client.__dict__.get('__abstractmethods__', 'absent')` you would see `'absent'`. Registration only affects `isinstance`/`issubclass` outcomes; it grants neither the attribute nor any abstractness semantics. ABC-aware introspection of registered classes requires `getattr(cls, '__abstractmethods__', frozenset())`.

Output:
```
class-attr
class-attr frozenset()
```

The abstract check only looks for a name override in the class namespace; a data attribute `data = 'class-attr'` is enough to clear it, so `Var()` works and prints `class-attr`. This confirms interfaces in Python are satisfied by *attributes* of any kind — methods, properties, class attributes, even plain data. It is a footgun if the interface intended callable behavior, since callers doing `v.data()` would crash with `TypeError: 'str' object is not callable`.

Output:
```
frozenset()
utility save
```

`Utility.save` sits earlier in the MRO than `App`'s abstract stub, so `RealApp`'s namespace lookup for `save` resolves to the concrete utility method. The metaclass sees a concrete `save` and clears the abstract set, and `RealApp` instantiates with `save` bound to `Utility.save`, printing `utility save`. This is exactly how mixins satisfy abstract interfaces: any class in the MRO that happens to carry the name counts, even if it was never designed as the ABC's implementation.

Output:
```
True True
['Real']
Can't instantiate abstract class Service without an implementation for abstract method 'run'
```

`Fake` passes `isinstance` purely because of `register` (virtual subclass), while `Real` passes as a genuine subclass — both are `True`. Only `Real` appears in `__subclasses__()`, showing registration forgery to type checks without touching the real hierarchy. The ABC itself shows its teeth last: no matter how many classes register or subclass it, `Service()` raises the familiar TypeError because its own `__abstractmethods__` still holds `'run'`. Formal checks see through the facade; instantiation does not.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
from abc import ABCMeta, abstractmethod
class A(metaclass=ABCMeta):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass
print(A.__abstractmethods__)
A()
questions.answer: Output: frozenset({'foo'}) followed by TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class A without an implementation for abstract method 'foo'. WHY: ABCMeta.__new__ scans the finished class namespace for descriptors whose __isabstractmethod__ is True and stores them in a frozenset assigned to the class attribute __abstractmethods__ AFTER the class object already exists (that is why you can print it on the class). A non-empty __abstractmethods__ marks the type as abstract, and the guard lives inside object.__new__, which raises TypeError at instantiation.

Output: 'raise on call' then AttributeError: __abstractmethods__. WHY: abstractmethod is only a function decorator that sets a marker attribute; a class using the default metaclass type ignores that marker, so A is never known to be abstract and instantiates normally. The failure happens only when you actually CALL foo, and __abstractmethods__ exists only if the metaclass is ABCMeta, hence the AttributeError here.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
from abc import ABCMeta, abstractmethod
class A(metaclass=ABCMeta):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass
class B:
    def foo(self): return 'hi'
A.register(B)
print(isinstance(B(), A))
print(issubclass(B, A))
print(B in A.__subclasses__())
questions.answer: Output: True / True / False. WHY: SomeABC.register(B) adds B to A's private virtual-subclass registry (a WeakSet) which ABCMeta.__instancecheck__ and __subclasscheck__ consult, so isinstance/issubclass become True WITHOUT any inheritance. The Python class graph is untouched, so A.__subclasses__() still lists only real subclasses, and B's __mro__ and __abstractmethods__ are unaffected.

Error: NameError: name 'A' is not defined. WHY: the class body executes while A is still being built, so the name A is not yet bound to the class object when @A.register runs. Fix: move the registration outside the class statement: A.register(B) (or the decorator form @A.register) after A exists.

Output: <class '__main__.B'> and True. WHY: register is a classmethod that returns the class it was given, so using it as a decorator is valid and leaves B unchanged. Registering marks B as a virtual subclass, making B() an instance of A from the isinstance point of view even though B does not inherit from A.

Output: TypeError: Can only register classes (twice, once for 3 and once for 'str'). WHY: register validates that its argument is a class because it must insert the argument into the ABC's weak-registry and be usable in issubclass/isinstance logic. Passing a non-class like an int or str is rejected up front with the same message.

questions.question:
Predict the output:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
class A(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def foo(self): pass
class B:
    def foo(self): return 1
b = B()
print(isinstance(b, A))
A.register(B)
print(isinstance(b, A))
questions.answer: Output: False then True. WHY: isinstance is evaluated at call time: ABCMeta.__instancecheck__ looks at type(b) and consults that class's registration status when you ask, not when the instance was created. The same b object becomes 'an A' only after B is registered, and its own __class__ never changes.

Output: False. WHY: for ABCMeta.__subclasscheck__, the __subclasshook__ result is checked FIRST and, if it is anything other than NotImplemented, that boolean is authoritative. Returning False from the hook therefore vetoes even classes that were explicitly registered with SomeABC.register — the registry is only consulted when the hook gives up with NotImplemented.
